paragraphs: Rabbi Elazar ben Arakh expounded the Chariot before his teacher Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai. Fire descended from heaven and surrounded them; ministering angels skipped before them like wedding companions rejoicing before a bridegroom. Another angel answered from the fire, “The Chariot is indeed as you say.” All the trees began singing, “Then all the trees of the forest shall sing.” Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai stood, kissed his head, and said, “Happy are you, our father Abraham, that Rabbi Elazar ben Arakh came from your loins,” Chagigah 14b; Jerusalem Talmud, beginning of Ein Doreshin. Avot de-Rabbi Natan, chapter 14: Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai called him a flowing stream, an ever-strengthening spring; Yuchasin writes “acute in argument.” See Avot, chapter 2: Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai praised him among his five students. See Asarah Ma'amarot [ע״מ; reading provisional]: he uprooted mountains (see Rabbi Eliezer the great). He died before his colleague, as Tosefta, Nedarim, chapter 6: Rabbi Yehoshua told Rabbi Akiva, “Alas, had you been in Rabbi Elazar ben Arakh’s days, would you have given this answer?” Some say he is Rabbi Elazar Hakkallir (see Rabbi Elazar son of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai). Kohelet Rabbah on “Oppression makes a wise man mad”: Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai had five students. While he lived they sat before him; when he died they went to Yavneh. Rabbi Elazar ben Arakh went to his wife at Emmaus, with fine water and a fine dwelling. He waited for them to come, but they did not. He wanted to go to them; his wife prevented him: “Who needs whom?” He said, “They need me.” She said, “The food-container and the mice—who normally goes to whom?”, etc. He listened, remained, and forgot his learning, etc.; he did not know why a relish was so named; see there. Shabbat, Chavit 147b: Rabbi Elazar ben Arakh (see Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai) came to Pogerita, with excellent wine, and Diyomset, whose salty waters warm and heal. Drawn after them, his learning was uprooted. On returning he rose to read “This month is for you” [החדש הזה לכם], but said “Deaf was their heart” [החרש היה לבם]. The sages prayed for him, and his learning returned. Thus the Mishnah: Rabbi Nehorai says, “Exile yourself to a place of Torah; do not say it will come after you,” etc. It is taught: his name was not Rabbi Nehorai, but Rabbi Nechemyah; some say Rabbi Elazar ben Arakh. Why Nehorai? He illuminates the sages’ eyes in law. (See Rabbi Nehorai.) Yalkut Reuveni, Toledot 50a; Bo 89; and the alphabetical entries, section 83, from Tzefunei Tziyyoni: “There is a husk named Riv [רי״ב], with 605 forces; it makes a sick person cease Torah study. The Name כד״ת, written on Messiah son of David’s forehead, nullifies all this.” End quotation. Rabbi Elazar ben Arakh (when ill and recovered—so Yalkut Reuveni in all three places; the Gemara lacks this, as above) changed the dalet of החדש to resh, zayin of הזה to yod, and kaf of לכם to bet: the letters רי״ב, hinting this harmful being caused it. החרש היה לבם has the numerical value 605, hinting its 605 forces. החדש הזה לכם has the numerical value כד״ת: it prevented him reading those words because this Name overcomes the harmful being and heals its harm. It says the Name is written on Messiah son of David’s forehead, not merely Messiah’s, because משיח בן דוד has the numerical value כד״ת. End quotation, in the name of the kabbalist Master Shimshon Maggid; it is wondrous. He spoke with Rabbi Zeira—very puzzling; see there. A synagogue in Damascus was traditionally said to have been built by Rabbi Elazar ben Arakh, Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai’s student; through an apostate it was destroyed in Mabbit’s days. See part II, book 2, section 99. Gelilot Eretz Yisrael writes: south of Kefar Alma, Rabbi Eliezer ben Hyrcanus is buried in a stone; nearby is a monument over Rabbi Shimon ben Netanel’s grave—some say Rabbi Yose the priest, some say Azaryah. Nearby is Rabbi Elazar ben Arakh’s grave, with monument, trees, fragrant fruit, a terebinth, and a vine. Among them is Rabbi Elazar ben Azaryah’s grave, with monument and terebinth. North of the village is Rabbi Yehudah ben Tema’s grave; nearby, a large cave with many caves containing Rabbah bar Rav Huna, Rav Hamnuna, Rav Chananel, and Rav Huna. (Elsewhere he writes burial at Ein Tzinah; perhaps there were two Rav Hunas.) It is called the Babylonians’ Cave. Benjamin’s Travels writes that Rabbi Elazar ben Arakh, Rabbi Elazar ben Azaryah, Choni the circle-drawer, Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, Rabbi Yose the Galilean, and Barak ben Avinoam are buried at Kedesh Naphtali.
